On 9 September 2026 I called Police Scotland on 101 from Falkirk, to report what I believe is ongoing fraud, account interference and related criminality affecting me.

This was not a new complaint. We have reported related matters for years: Proton Mail accounts used to send court and tribunal material; X and Facebook accounts created, blocked or appearing in our names; Royal Bank of Scotland issues on  debit account (including what the bank described as high-level / “Grade 4” controls); delivery notifications for parcels in Ayrshire while we lived in Aberdeen; credit cards, a driving licence and other items found in properties we occupied; property damage and alleged unauthorised entry; and court / Housing and Property Chamber processes in which we say documents we sent were not received as sent, or came back as incoherent download-folder versions rather than the papers we actually submitted.

The immediate reason for the 9 September call was a new X account I set up about two days earlier. When we tried to take a Premium subscription and selected payment by “Link”, the flow populated an old phone number and the same long compromised email address we have been reporting as hacked. That account should not have held those details. We asked for officers to attend so they could see the screens, recordings and other material rather than deal with it only by phone.

The advisor took my name, the contact number ending XXX, and the address at XX XXXXXXXX XXXXX, Falkirk. After a long hold, the call was logged as an incident for officers to come out. I asked that it go to fraud / CID and that the bank also be notified. I was told that who attends is not the call-handler’s decision and that officers would take the detail in person. I was also told the call centre was busy and that I had already been on the line for a long time.

No meaningful investigatory process followed from that call, which matches a pattern we have described before: concern at first contact, then no forensic examination of devices, mail logs, bank audit trails, CCTV, or the items found in the house; no proper follow-up with RBS; and previous Aberdeen inquiries (including matters we raised with an officer we named as PC XXXXXXXX) written up in ways that did not match the evidence we handed over.

Public bodies are involved: Police Scotland, Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service / sheriff courts and the Housing and Property Chamber, Aberdeen and Falkirk councils in the background of housing and statements, and a major high street bank. Those organisations can be scrutinised. We are not asking the public to treat every allegation as already proved. We are asking that the digital and paper trail be tested in the open.

Proton Mail and court-email metadata: what was sent, what clerks received, and why returned papers matched download folder templates rather than the filed versions.
X / Link payment data on a days-old account that surfaced old numbers and a previously reported email.
RBS Grade 4 / fraud logs and why I could not get a manager meeting or a clear account of unrecognised activity.
Chain of custody for cards and other items found at addresses, including who entered when, CCTV gaps, and why a gas engineer would already know about cards.
Whether statements attributed to named officials in tribunal/court papers were actually made by those people.

I have submitted a formal complaint. I want that complaint secured in the process: a recorded incident number, written confirmation of what was logged on 9 September 2026, a named investigating unit (not only a local attendance that never becomes a cyber/fraud file), preservation of devices and recordings, and a Subject Access / production route to bank and platform logs rather than another closed door.

If Police Scotland, the bank and the courts say nothing criminal occurred, they can say so with the logs. If the material supports unauthorised access, interference with correspondence to courts, or fraud, it should be investigated as such—not absorbed into “no crime / user error / vexatious caller.”

We will provide officers and any independent reviewer with the recordings of the 101 call, the X payment screens, the court correspondence we retained, and the other material we have already offered. Public bodies should not be able to end this solely by not attending, not seizing exhibits, and not writing a reasoned decision.

What would you do if you repetitively  recorded police covering up the crimes whilst attempting to make it look as if they are performing their duties?

Let me tell you what we done. We moved to the northeast of Scotland, to the villages of Boddam, and then on to Aberdeen, to various addresses. We got up in the mornings, stayed up all night to record evidence: people who were being handled by letting agents and landlords, orchestrated by people in authority, in order to bring false claims against us. 

This manifests into 6 years of racism, hate crime, and organised crime. The evidence that I have collected, the police have never seen, as they would never attend. On attendance, they would be manipulative, controlling, threatening, abusive.

You're still found guilty on some of the most horrific organised crime development of people who were following us about Aberdeen consistently, but recorded the backside out of it, only for them to procure a woman who had been attacking us for many, many months, along with her family, who worked in a superstore, to follow us about the town and then eventually get the dogs killed as a result of her actions. FG Shuts Over 13 Million Social Media Accounts, Deletes 59 Million Offens+ve Posts

The code, jointly issued by the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), and the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC), outlines measures to curb online h@rm.

text:
PUBLIC LEGAL NOTICE

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

2. THE GRIEVANCE OFFICER & LEGAL CELL
  Meta Platforms, Inc. / Instagram LLC
  (Intermediary hosting subject digital broadcast)

3. TO WHOMSOEVER IT MAY CONCERN / GENERAL PUBLIC
SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

quotedTweet.text:
I have filed a complaint with the Grievance Officer of YouTube against those bloggers as per the IT Rules, as directed by the Delhi High Court. The time limit for the Grievance Officer to act on the complaint is 15 days from the date of receipt. If YouTube does not take action, there is a Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) where we can challenge the decision of the Grievance Officer. The GAC has a 30-day time limit to resolve the complaint or take action.

The Hon'ble Acting Chief Justice advised me, while disposing of the PIL, to follow this mechanism. If I am not satisfied with the GAC's decision, I may approach the Court again.

I have identified a total of 33 YouTube channels that are posting videos of women and minor girls in a demeaning manner, with 589 such videos identified so far. Although these bloggers continue to post such content, I must follow the prescribed mechanism.

I will adhere to this process and will approach the Court again if the desired action is not taken by the Grievance Officer or the Grievance Appellate Committee.

🛢️ What exactly is India sending to Russia?
1. Oil and fuels
India purchases Russian oil at significant discounts and then sells the resulting fuels on global markets, including to Europe. Although this practice is legal—since the fuel is no longer classified as "Russian"—it economically bolsters Russia by providing a buyer for its raw materials.

2. Dual-use goods

electronics,

3. Technologies and components for the defense industry

🔍 How does India circumvent sanctions?
1. Re-export via intermediary companies
India purchases goods from the West, assembles or repackages them, and then ships them to Russia. This makes detecting the practice difficult, as the transaction is not formally classified as a direct export from the EU to Russia. 2. Purchase of Russian oil via intermediaries

3. Large-scale trade

🧭 Why is India doing this?

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Many journalists, politicians, and creators in India are facing similar issues; accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected. She said the journalists were accused of being Muslim and a doctor at the hospital openly displayed bias. 

On Sept 6 the social media accounts of Bindu Gurjar, Lok Singh and Monika were suspended. Monika's account is still suspended. "We are independent journalists," she said, "how will we earn and continue to work if accounts are suspended?" 

Impassioned testimonies came from Shaheen Khan and Nafeesa Khan of 4 PM News, who were picked up by Saket police on Sept 3, 2026, while standing on the roadside to report the visit of Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta to Max Hospital to inaugurate a new wing. 
 
Nafeesa described in detail their detention at Saket police station and the trauma of being beaten with fists and a lathi by a woman inspector. She said she began to fear for her life after the inspector learnt they were Muslim and began to beat them more viciously. The SHO, she said, had ordered the beating and other police personnel were complicit. 

Shaheen said that after the incident became public senior policemen later apologised and admitted there had been a mistake. However, she said, the FIR eventually registered names of only two police personnel, although they have filed a complaint against several personnel. She urged journalists to take up the issue and ensure justice.

The meeting was also addressed by PCI President Sangeeta Baruah Pisharoty, Secretary General Afzal Imam, DUJ President Sujata Madhok, Divya Arya of the Network of Women Journalists in India, journalist Khushbu Akhtar and Caravan Editor Hartosh Singh Bal who expressed solidarity with the media women and applauded them for their courage in speaking out.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. About Krasner—I have been a Philly government whistleblower for 20 years and several times reactivated against. Had to move out but still ill from what they did to me. Following is just a small part of the what had happened. 

I sent evidence to Krasner to get a port-conviction review for Sean Benschop—who has been in jail for the demolition accident at Market Street, June 5, 2013.

My troubles with the construction project adjacent to my house that cracked my hours and poisoned me with lead and mercury were doing demolition with no permits—among other permit failures. I have a copy of that violation that led to the shutdown.

By the time of the Markert Street demolition, I knew a lot because I spent years going to meetings and learning safety regs and sending the city's very own safety regs to the city. I got to know top people in city planning very well, and they knew me. Including the deputy mayor Alan Greenburg, who is also big at city planning.

Around the fall of 2011, we were both at a symposium presented by the Public Interest Law Center that featured Vernice Travis Miller, who worked on a demolition protocol in Baltimore in conjunction with Johns Hopkins, covering the health aspect of demolition.

In 2006—soon after I was ill from both the demolition dust and lead and mercury from the site next to my house (by 6 feet)—I attended a meeting in the Northern Liberties neighborhood that was organized by Hilary Regan. The feature speaker there was also presenting the same Balitmore demolition safety protocols. Many city officials were at that meeting, mainly from city planning and licenses and inspections, and Department of Environmental Protection.

We were all given the Balitmore demolition safety protocols. One of the first things in that publication was "REMOVE EVERYONE IN THE ADJACENT AREA BUILDING NEXT TO ACTIVE DEMOLITION."

The same Manuel and other person who worked on the Baltimore protocols was presented at the Fall 2011 symposium. I was there, and Alan Greenburger—the deputy mayor—was there. Everyone got a copy of the safety protocols.

Just before the symposium, the police came to my door-- a tempplace I was living because I could no longer live in my house, where I had become the target of many crimes, and the local police had been informed to never help me—plus the poor air quality that continually put me in a hospital.

So the police came to my door and showed me an email I had Alan Greenburger tell him about the meeting on demolition safety and related topics presented by the Public Interest Law Center. The police asked me if I had written the email and if I was going to the meeting. I said yes, I had paid for my ticket, and there was no reason why I should not go.

Police at my door asking about me going to this meeting??!!

I went, and Alan Greenburg showed up and sat up front next to the featured speaker, Vrenice Travis Miller, and interacted with her verbally. I have the court reporter transcript of that meeting so I can prove that.

I was always polite at meetings, and I said nothing at that meeting—except during a break. I politely turned to another person—most were lawyers—and told her a bit about my situation. She was hostile and said nobody was ever going to help me. Later, I found out that one of their top lawyers had something to do with that land next to my house—but I don't have sure evidence, so I will not say—but that organization in many ways has sabotaged all along.

About that same month a woman died in a flood that a retired water engineer pointed at the project next to my house and said the building on top of the creek that was under that land was a flood danger. At the 2006 meeting, I brought the stream map and showed City Planning the same thing and told them it was a danger. One dead.

Then deputy mayor Alan Greenburger spent a couple of months emailing (I have some copies of those) back and forth about the Salvation Army and the demo project. He was the professional. He had the safety protocols about not doing demos next to any building with people in it. He had been hearing about demo danger and all the other dangers for years from me. ALL HE HAD TO DO WAS ORDER SOME WARNING SIGNS PUT UP AND SOME BARRIERS ON THE SIDEWALK TO SAY DANGER.

He did not—so a bunch more people died that day. And later on national TV, Mayor Nutter, surrounded by a group of city officials, many of whom I had talked to about my demo and lead and mercury problems—including Alan Greenburg—stood together, and Mayor Nutter told the world on national TV that Philadelphia did not know much about demolition.

I gave all this info to Krasner and asked for a post-conviction for the demolition driver who was obeying orders from his boss. I had heard Krasner was into post conviction. text:
Okay. Let me walk you through what happened.

On 31 August 2026, Malesela Teffo arrived at the Johannesburg High Court during Cat Matlala's attempted murder trial.

He was not on the case. He was not representing anyone. He walked in unannounced and asked to intervene — as a "friend of the court," or through his Pro Bono Foundation, claiming constitutional violations.

Judge Cassim Moosa told him to produce proof of readmission from the LPC or the High Court. Teffo could not.

The application was stood down.

Then the police arrived.

Here is what you need to understand before the headlines write themselves.

1. Teffo is not a lawyer anymore.

He was admitted as an advocate in 2009. But in September 2022, the Pretoria High Court struck him off the roll following an application by the Legal Practice Council.

The court cited serious professional misconduct: misappropriating client funds, taking briefs directly from clients without instructing attorneys, misleading courts, breaching court orders.

These were not allegations. These were findings of a court.

And in July 2026, he was acquitted of six criminal charges — assault, fraud-related matters, incidents from 2023. The LPC made clear: acquittal does not restore your right to practise. An acquittal says the state did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It does not erase a striking-off order.

He remains struck off. He is not entitled to appear in court or offer legal services.

2. The warrant was already in the system.

The LPC confirmed a warrant of arrest existed, stemming from a prior contempt finding. A 2023/2024 court order declared him in contempt of the original striking-off order, with a suspended 12-month imprisonment sentence if he complied.

Police had previously been unable to locate him.

Then he walked into a courtroom.

3. Now the context matters.

The trial he interrupted was Cat Matlala's — the same Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala who won the R360 million SAPS medical tender that was later confirmed as irregular expenditure, with at least R50 million already paid before cancellation.

Matlala has been arrested on corruption and fraud charges. The charges against Police Commissioner Masemola linked to that tender were just dropped by the NPA.

Teffo is not a random bystander in this story.

He is a former defence counsel in the Senzo Meyiwa trial who gained prominence through that high-profile exposure. He positioned himself as a constitutional watchdog. And he showed up at the courtroom of a man whose tender was built on the same rot that the Madlanga Commission is currently mapping.

4. Here is the uncomfortable part.

A struck-off advocate appearing during a corruption trial does not raise the same question it would if the accused were a nobody.

When you remove yourself from the rolls of legal practitioners, when you are in contempt of the order that removed you, when a warrant is already circulating — and then you choose that moment to walk into that courtroom and ask to intervene...

The timing does not read like constitutional activism.

It reads like someone who knows which courtroom will get cameras.

5. That does not mean the constitutional questions he raised are wrong.

It does not mean the accused should not get a fair trial. It does not mean the state cannot abuse process.

But it does mean we should be clear about what this is.

It is not an advocate defending the rule of law.

It is a man who has been told by two separate courts that he cannot practise law, walking into a high-profile corruption trial and asking to be heard.

The judge did not hear him. The police did.

The uncomfortable truth:

The rule of law does not need protectors who are themselves subject to warrants.

A struck-off advocate appearing in court is not a constitutional crisis.

It is a man who forgot that the order striking him off was not a suggestion.

And the warrant that finally found him was not new.

It had been waiting.

#Teffo #CatMatlala #MadlangaCommission

Foreign VPNs have often been found involved in planning & execution of terror activities, funding, facilitation and radicalisation of youth and crime against children & women by spread of p€rverted content & therefore the biggest threat to the nation's security and culture. Below is my letter to GOI seeking an immediate ban on foreign VPNs & detailing instances of their blatant misuse for:

A. Terrorism and radicalisation
B. Crime against children and women
C. Financial fraud
D. Drug trafficking
E. Extortion, blackmailing, etc.

In my letter I have listed a sample of 50 serious instances of these crimes and terror activities from India and around the world.

Below is the full text of the letter :

10th November 2025

Shri Amit Shah
Union Home Minister

Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw
Union Minister of Electronics and Information Technology

Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal
Union Minister of State (I/C) for Law & Justice

Smt Annpurna Devi
Union Minister of Women and Child Development

Sub: Urgent Request for Immediate Nationwide Ban on Foreign VPN Services to Curb Crimes Against Children, Women, Drug Trafficking, Financial Fraud, and Threats to National Security

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

Despite the mandatory 5-year logging requirement imposed on VPN providers under these directions, major foreign VPNs—NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, ProtonVPN, Mullvad, and others—have openly refused compliance by removing physical servers from India and routing traffic through virtual IPs abroad. This deliberate non-cooperation has turned these services into safe havens for criminals and terrorists operating in and targeting India.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

The list of crimes and terror-related incidents involving VPNs is long. We are listing below just a few recent examples of how VPNs were used to commit crimes against children and women, plan terrorist activities, traffic drugs and conduct fraud. Each incident lists the crime, VPN use, and primary-source link [U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) / Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) / European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) / The International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)].

Crimes Against Children (VPN-Enabled Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) Cases)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs (or VPN + Tor) to hide while committing Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) related crimes—downloading, sharing, or live-streaming.

1. Connecticut, USA – 2025
Michael Hull (61) used paid VPN + Tor for 4 years to access dark-web CSAM. FBI traced via VPN IP leak → DOJ
2. Minnesota, USA – Operation Grayskull, 2025
Thomas Katsampes (52) ran a 2,000-user CSAM forum requiring VPN + Tor hopping. FBI de-anonymized 18 admins via logs → DOJ
3. Florida, USA – Playpen Network, 2023–2025
956 arrests; 214 used NordVPN/PIA/Mullvad + Tor. FBI NIT malware captured real IPs on CSAM clicks → FBI
4. Germany – Boystown Takedown, 2021 (ongoing 2023 arrests)
400,000 users; rules mandated VPN + Tor. BKA arrested 72; 2 VPN providers surrendered logs under EU warrants → BKA/Europol
5. South Korea – Welcome to Video, 2019–2024
337 arrests; 41 used VPN exits in Sweden/Romania for Bitcoin CSAM buys. IRS traced VPN payments → DOJ
6. Australia – Childs Play, 2016–2017 (2023 follow-ups)
1.1M users; admin taught 3-VPN chaining + Tor. Task Force Argos caught 94 via VPN leaks → Queensland Police
7. Latin America – Operation Vibora, 2025
20 arrests; suspects used free mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder) for live-streamed child rape. VPN logs seized → Interpol
8. Oklahoma, USA – Thomas Gailus, 2025
Repeat offender used dark web via VPN to collect CSAM of prepubescents. 10-year sentence → DOJ
9. Washington, USA – Operation Restore Justice, 2025
Mitchell Dufault distributed CSAM via VPN-masked platforms. 10-year sentence → DOJ
10. Arizona, USA – 22 Defendants, 2023–2025
Multiple offenders used VPNs for CSAM possession/distribution. Charges under Project Safe Childhood → DOJ

Crimes Against Women (VPN-Enabled Cyberstalking/Sextortion)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs for cyberstalking, sextortion, or non-consensual porn against women.

1. Massachusetts, USA – James Florence Jr, 2025
Cyberstalked 13 women with paid VPNs for deepfake nudes/rape threats. 9-year sentence → DOJ
2. Albuquerque, USA – Phillip Gonzales, 2025
Sent rape-fantasy texts to 7 women via VPN-chained VoIP. VPN logs seized → DOJ
3. Global – 911 S5 Botnet, 2025
YunHe Wang sold VPN-proxied IPs for 4,000+ sextortion/rape threats against women. Servers seized → DOJ
4. Los Angeles, USA – Kody Roberts, 2023
Sent rape/murder threats to 3 women via commercial VPN. NIT grabbed IP → DOJ
5. Florida, USA – Christopher Buonocore, 2021–2024
Sextorted dozens, hired rapists via NordVPN + Tor. Bitcoin traces led to arrest → DOJ
6. Washington DC, USA – Nahvarj Mills, 2024
Posted revenge porn via Swedish VPN exits. 27-count indictment → DOJ
7. Naperville, USA – Cody Ratliff, 2025
Sextorted teen girl via mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder). Logs handed over → Police
8. California, USA – Chavarri Sextortion, 2019–2021 (2025 arrest)
Stalked/harassed women via VPN-masked accounts for nudes → DOJ
9. Global – Financial Sextortion Surge, 2023–2025
Overseas offenders used VPNs for anonymous threats; 33.5M losses → FinCEN/FBI
10. Nigeria – Operation Artemis, 2025
22 arrests for sextortion using VPNs to mask ops; 54K teen victims → FBI

Terrorism (VPN-Enabled Plots/Propaganda)

Here are 10 cases where terrorists used VPNs for propaganda, recruitment, or planning.

1. ISIS Global Propaganda – 2024
9 admins ran 150+ servers with https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM mandatory. FBI/Europol seized; logs exposed → FBI/Europol
2. Terrorgram Collective – 2024
Leaders used Mullvad + Tor for kill lists/bomb manuals. Payment slip traced → DOJ
3. Al-Qaeda Inspire Distributors – 2023–2025
14-cell used https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM for bomb tutorials. 3-year logs seized → Europol
4. Hamas Crypto-Fundraising – 2025
3 operatives laundered $2M via DoubleVPN Sweden exits. Logs identified wallets → DOJ
5. ISIS Sniper Channel – Minnesota, 2025
Abdelhamid Hassan uploaded 200+ videos via Safe-Inet VPN. Logs showed 18 US IPs → DOJ
6. The Base Bomb Cell – Germany/USA, 2024
5 neo-Nazis plotted via Insorg VPN C2. Logs named all → DOJ/Europol
7. Hamas Live-Stream Recruiters – Spain, 2025
9 operatives streamed via VPN-chained apps. Turbo VPN logs revealed 73 → Eurojust
8. EU Jihadist Plots – 2023–2024
24 plots (6 attacks) used VPNs for online radicalization post-Hamas Oct 7 → Europol TE-SAT
9. Al-Qaeda Online Jihad – 2023
Propaganda surge via VPN-masked uploads after Zawahiri death → Europol
10. Hamas/Al-Qassam Finance – 2025
3 campaigns dismantled; VPNs obscured cyber-finance for arms → DOJ

Other Serious Threats (VPN-Enabled Ransomware/Fraud/Etc.)

Here are 10 cases of VPN use in ransomware, hacks, fraud, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking (no overlap with prior categories).

1. ALPHV/BlackCat – US Firms, 2023
3 hackers used Mullvad/ProtonVPN for $5M ransomware. Wallet traced → DOJ
2. LockBit Hospital Attacks – TX/CA, 2024
Teen chained Nord/ExpressVPN to encrypt MRIs; 400GB leaked. Servers seized → Europol
3. $20M Real-Estate Fraud – 400 Homes, 2021–2024
Nigerian gang used IPVanish/Surfshark to divert wires. $3.2M seized → DOJ
4. Iranian Murder-for-Hire – NYC, 2024
IRGC hitmen used https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM for $100K Bitcoin scouting. Logs seized → DOJ
5. DoubleVPN – 100+ Gangs, 2019–2021
Conti/REvil used DoubleVPN for C2; 2.5K exposed via 2TB logs → Europol
6. Safe-Inet – Hive/Dharma, 2020–2025
71-country hits; Safe-Inet mandatory. BKA warrant on logs → Europol
7. Dark-Web Fentanyl Cartel – 50K Deaths, 2023–2025
Pharma-Master used VPNLab/Mullvad for 12 markets; 34 arrests → DOJ
8. DoppelPaymer Ransomware – 37 Attacks, 2023
Ukrainian core used VPNs for €10M hospital hacks (Düsseldorf). 5 arrested → Europol
9. Operation RapTor – Dark Web Drugs, 2025
288 vendors arrested; VPNs masked trafficking. €184M seized → Europol
10. MATRIX Encrypted Platform – 2024
Drug/arms/murder-for-hire via VPN-integrated comms. 2.3M messages intercepted → Europol

Foreign VPN Use in Crimes in India (2020–2025)

Here are 10 news reports from 2020–2025 detailing cases where foreign VPNs (or non-compliant international VPN services) were used to commit or facilitate crimes against children (CSAM/pornography), women (sextortion/cyberstalking), terrorism/national security threats, or other serious offenses (ransomware/fraud/drug trafficking) in India. Each includes a brief summary, crime type, and primary source link.

1. Sharp Rise in CSAM Demand via VPNs (2020)
During COVID-19 lockdown, ICPF report noted a 100% surge in child pornography searches (5M/month across 100 cities), with users employing foreign VPNs to bypass India's CSAM bans.
Crime: Child exploitation → Times of India
2. 25,000 CSAM Uploads Traced, VPNs Suspected in Access (2020)
NCMEC alerted NCRB to 25,000 child pornography uploads from India (Delhi tops list); offenders used foreign VPNs to access dark web sites, leading to FIRs and arrests in multiple states.
Crime: Child pornography distribution → The Indian Express
3. Kerala P-Hunt Operation: 47 Arrests for Dark Web CSAM (2020)
Kerala Police's covert op arrested 47 (including youth) for downloading child abuse material via foreign VPNs on darknet during lockdown; surge linked to encrypted access tools.
Crime: Child sexual abuse material → India Today
4. Porn Blackmail via VPN-Tracked Footprints (2020)
Mumbai racketeers used foreign VPNs to track porn viewers' digital footprints, then extorted bitcoins threatening exposure; cyber cell devising VPN blocks for such crimes.
Crime: Sextortion/extortion against adults (linked to child porn access) → Mumbai Mirror
5. Nagpur: 30 Arrests in 38 CSAM Cases via VPN Access (2021)
City police arrested 30 in 38 child pornography cases based on cyber intel; offenders used international VPNs to browse dark net/paid sites, prompted by NCCRP tips.
Crime: Child pornography possession → Times of India
6. Telangana: 43 Arrested for CSAM Circulation via VPNs (2023)
Cyber Crime wing arrested 43 using tip lines; suspects employed foreign VPNs to upload/share child sexual abuse material on social media/dark web.
Crime: Child pornography trafficking → The Hindu
7. Gorakhnath Temple Attack: ISIL Funding via PayPal & VPNs (2022, reported 2025)
Accused used foreign VPNs to obscure IP while transferring ₹6.7L via PayPal to ISIL supporters abroad for terror planning; FATF highlighted as national security threat.
Crime: Terrorism financing → The Hindu
8. Flight Bomb Hoax Threats via VPN-Masked IPs (2024)
Over 150 Delhi flights received hoax bomb threats on X; sender used foreign VPNs (IPs traced to London/Germany) to hide origin, complicating national security probes.
Crime: Terrorism hoax/threat to aviation security → India Today
9. Scamsters Use Rented Foreign VPNs for Ransomware/Phishing (2023)
Gujarat fraudsters rented VPNs from Marshall Islands/Australia to mask ops in ransomware, card fraud, and sextortion targeting Indians; evaded extradition via non-treaty nations.
Crime: Ransomware/financial fraud → Times of India
10. Bengaluru Rs 49Cr Fraud: Foreign Hackers Use VPN for Mule Accounts (2025)
Hackers from abroad used VPNs to breach Whizdm Finance's API, siphoning ₹49Cr via 100s of transactions; locals arrested for creating VPN-masked mule accounts.
Crime: Cyber fraud/ransomware-like theft → Times of India

Sir, the pattern is undeniable:

- Foreign VPNs openly defy Indian law.
- They enable child exploitation, pornography, violence against women, radicalization, drug trafficking and terrorist activity.

Requested Immediate Possible Actions for Consideration:

1. Publish a National Registry of Compliant VPNs
Direct CERT-In and MeitY to publish and maintain a public registry of VPN providers that have demonstrated compliance with the 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Requirement: Five-year data logging, real-time incident reporting, and appointment of an Indian-resident nodal officer.
Purpose: Establish transparency and a verifiable compliance benchmark for enforcement.

2. Delist and Prohibit Operation of Non-Compliant Foreign VPNs
Instruct Apple, Google, and all Indian ISPs to immediately delist and block all non-compliant foreign VPNs, including NordVPN, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and Mullvad, that have refused to adhere to the 2022 CERT-In Directions.
Action: To be taken under the blocking powers of the Information Technology Act and its associated Intermediary Guidelines.
Purpose: Prevent evasion of Indian jurisdiction and close routes for offenders hiding behind virtual foreign IPs.

3. Block Associated Payment Channels
Direct the Reserve Bank of India and all licensed payment aggregators and card networks such as PayU, Razorpay, Visa, and Mastercard to suspend or block subscription transactions to banned or non-compliant VPN providers.
Purpose: Cut off domestic funding and revenue flows sustaining illegal VPN operations.

4. Mandate Exclusive Use of CERT-In Certified VPNs
Require, through regulatory notification, that only VPNs, whether Indian or foreign, that obtain CERT-In certification be permitted to operate in India.
All VPNs advertising Indian IP services must maintain logging infrastructure within Indian jurisdiction and comply with lawful requests from enforcement agencies.
Purpose: Ensure traceability and lawful accountability of all VPN activity associated with Indian IP addresses.

5. Criminalise Intentional Use for Concealment During Offences
Propose suitable amendments or notifications under the Information Technology Act and India’s relevant penal codes to criminalise the intentional use of banned or non-compliant VPNs for concealing identity during the commission of cognisable offences involving child sexual abuse material, terrorism, radicalisation, or financial fraud.
Purpose: Target deliberate misuse while preserving lawful privacy.

6. Strengthen Traceability and Cooperation
Mandate that every VPN provider operating in India:
(a) Designate a resident nodal officer;
(b) Retain subscriber and metadata for five years; and
(c) Respond to law enforcement requests within seventy-two hours, as required by the CERT-In Directions of 2022.
Purpose: Guarantee swift investigatory access while preserving due process.

7. Establish a National Honeypot and Canarytoken Programme
Authorise CERT-In and the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit to deploy a nationwide honeypot and Canarytoken framework, as validated in peer-reviewed research, to trace VPN-enabled crimes involving child sexual abuse material, sextortion, ransomware, and terror financing.
Ensure judicial oversight, privacy protection, and certified chain of custody for admissibility of digital evidence.
Purpose: Build indigenous technical capability to unmask offenders using VPN anonymity.

8. Strengthen International Coordination and FATF Alignment
Direct NIA, CBI, and MHA’s Cyber Coordination Centre to:
(a) Formalise fast-track cooperation with FBI, Europol, and Interpol under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties; and
(b) Report VPN-linked money-laundering or terror-financing incidents to the Financial Action Task Force in conformity with its Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks dated 8 July 2025.
Purpose: Integrate India’s enforcement with global counter-terror and cybercrime frameworks.

9. Institute Annual CERT-In Audit and Enforcement Schedule
Require annual audits of VPN providers’ compliance and publish audit summaries for public accountability.
Providers failing to comply beyond sixty days after notice should face permanent blocking and notifications to RBI, DoT, and MeitY for coordinated enforcement.
Purpose: Ensure continuous oversight and eliminate recurring non-compliance.

10. Issue a Public Advisory and Compliance Deadline
Issue a national advisory within thirty days, notifying all VPN providers of a sixty-day compliance window.
After the deadline, non-compliant entities should face delisting, domain blocking, and payment interdiction without exception.
Purpose: Provide procedural fairness before enforcement action begins.

India must not remain a playground for foreign tools that shield sexual predators, criminals and terrorists. The Ministry of Home Affairs has already acted strictly—forcing Apple and Google to delist 6+ non-compliant VPNs in January 2025. It is time to complete the job.

Vande Mataram

Uday Mahurkar
Founder, Save Culture Save Bharat Foundation
Former Central Information Commissioner, Government of India

@Meta @NCPCR @MeitY @JoelKaplan Tracked by Press Monitor — today's press review covers four major developments in social media regulation and platform governance.

Meta has agreed to report child safety cases directly to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, bypassing the US-based NCMEC.
